title: How I Price Every New Offer
transcript: There's called the Van Wesson door pricing analysis. I do this most times when I launch a new offering. There's four questions you ask. Number one, at what price would this be so expensive that you wouldn't even consider it. Number two, at what price would this be so cheap that it would be impossible that it would be able to be valuable? At what price would it be right at the edge? You'd have to really consider it, but you'd end up buying it. And then at what price would it be a bargain, a good deal? So, when I run these, I ask those four questions, but I also ask for the customer stats. So, then I can slice it by saying, what do the rich customers think? What's the pricing curve for them? What's the pricing curve for poor customers? And so then you can get really really accurate with initial pricing.

title: Sell To Better Customers
transcript: If you increase the quality of your prospects, you will increase the quality of your product. At Gym Launch, we figured out that gym owners that were the most successful had three things in common. A signed lease, they had at least one employee. They had at least 30 customers. So, if someone has all three of those things, they'll make a ton of money with our thing. We told the sales team then. We said, "If they don't have these three things, do not sell them." We told the marketing team, "Say this in all of our marketing. If they don't have these three things, tell them this is not for them." So, what happened? We sold better people. Guess what happened after that? Our average results went up. Guess what we could do after that? Market average better results. And what do we do? Get better customers. is it becomes a virtuous cycle that improves the product. Here's the crazy part. We didn't actually change anything about what we sold.
